questions.title: Delegate the right task
questions.question: Which task is appropriate for the registered nurse to delegate to an assistive personnel on a stable ward patient?
options: Obtaining routine vital signs on a stable patient and reporting the results
Carrying out the admission assessment for a newly arrived patient
Teaching a newly diagnosed patient how to draw up their insulin
Interpreting a change in a patient's neurological observations
questions.rationale: Routine, repeatable tasks with a predictable outcome on a stable patient may be delegated, but the nurse remains accountable for the decision and the follow-up. Assessment, teaching, interpretation of clinical data and anything requiring nursing judgement stay with the registered nurse.
questions.sourceTitle: NCSBN: National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation
questions.learningObjective: Delegate only tasks that are routine and predictable, and keep assessment and judgement with the registered nurse.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated ward scene: an assistive worker writes a routine observation on a board while a registered nurse reviews a chart nearby; no readable text or numbers.

questions.title: Least restrictive option
questions.question: A confused adult is pulling at their intravenous cannula. Which response reflects the least restrictive approach before any physical restraint is considered?
options: Apply wrist restraints straight away so the cannula cannot be pulled out
Sedate the patient so the cannula site can be protected
Ask a colleague to hold the patient's arm continuously for the whole shift
Try reorientation, distraction, moving the cannula site and involving family before considering restraint
questions.rationale: Any restriction of liberty must be proportionate and the least restrictive option for the shortest time, so simpler measures such as reorientation, distraction, relocating the cannula and family involvement come first. Restriction is a last resort that requires proper legal authority, review and record-keeping.
questions.sourceTitle: Mental Capacity Act 2005 Code of Practice (UK Government)
questions.learningObjective: Use the least restrictive option and exhaust simpler measures before any restraint.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated bay with a cannula dressed on a blanket roll on an empty bed, a relative's chair pulled close and a familiar object on the bedside table; no people.

questions.title: First response to fire
questions.question: A small fire starts in a ward utility room. According to the RACE sequence, what should the nurse do first?
options: Close all doors and windows before doing anything else
Start evacuating the entire ward immediately
Rescue anyone in immediate danger and activate the alarm
Fetch the nearest extinguisher and fight the fire alone
questions.rationale: RACE stands for Rescue anyone in immediate danger, Activate the alarm, Contain the fire, then Extinguish or Evacuate as trained. People come before property, and no nurse is expected to fight a fire before patients and colleagues are safe and the alarm has been raised.
questions.sourceTitle: Nursing Fundamentals 2e (Open RN, WisTech Open, CC BY 4.0, 2024)
questions.learningObjective: Follow the RACE sequence, beginning with rescuing people in immediate danger.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated utility-room doorway with an alarm call point on the wall and a fire door, rendered as a clean illustration; no flames and no readable signage.

questions.title: Confusion is a symptom
questions.question: An older adult has become acutely confused overnight and had no cognitive problems previously. What should the nurse's assessment focus on first?
options: Moving the patient to a side room and observing for 24 hours before acting
Searching for reversible causes such as infection, pain, dehydration, constipation and new medication changes
Confirming a diagnosis of dementia so the care plan can be updated
Scheduling a routine review with the mental health team next week
questions.rationale: Acute new confusion suggests delirium, which usually has a reversible trigger such as infection, pain, dehydration, constipation, urinary retention or a new drug. Treating the underlying cause is the priority, because delirium is often preventable and reversible, unlike most dementia.
questions.sourceTitle: NICE guideline CG103: Delirium - prevention, diagnosis and management
questions.learningObjective: Treat acute confusion as delirium until reversible causes have been excluded.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated bedside observation tray with a water jug, medication trolley in the background and an observation chart folder, all with blurred unreadable labels; no people.

questions.title: Score, then escalate
questions.question: A patient's early-warning observations are trending worse across the shift. What should the nurse do with the score?
options: Wait until a full set of observations has been completed three times before reporting
Report only the abnormal respiratory rate and leave the rest out of handover
Reassure the patient and repeat the observations at the next routine time
Calculate the aggregate early-warning score and escalate according to the threshold the score reaches
questions.rationale: Track-and-trigger systems such as NEWS2 score each parameter and set an escalation threshold, so a rising aggregate score prompts a graded clinical response rather than waiting for routine review. A trend across observations is as important as a single abnormal value.
questions.sourceTitle: Royal College of Physicians: National Early Warning Score (NEWS2)
questions.learningObjective: Escalate a rising early-warning score at the threshold, not at the next routine round.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated nurse completing observations on a wall-mounted monitor with the numbers blurred, escalation phone in hand; no identifiable faces.

questions.title: Stop the trigger, then adrenaline
questions.question: A patient develops a widespread rash, facial swelling and difficulty breathing minutes after a medicine infusion begins. What is the nurse's priority?
options: Wait for intravenous access to be established before starting any treatment
Slow the infusion and reassess the patient in fifteen minutes
Stop the suspected trigger, call for help and prepare intramuscular adrenaline per the anaphylaxis protocol
Give an oral antihistamine first and observe the response
questions.rationale: A rapid-onset reaction with airway, breathing or circulation involvement is treated as anaphylaxis: remove the suspected trigger, call for help and give intramuscular adrenaline early per protocol. Antihistamines and observation are not a substitute, and treatment never waits on perfect intravenous access.
questions.sourceTitle: Resuscitation Council UK: Anaphylaxis guideline (2021)
questions.learningObjective: Recognise anaphylaxis, remove the trigger and escalate for intramuscular adrenaline immediately.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated infusion stand paused with the line clamped and an emergency call bell pressed, drawn as an illustration; no patient body and no readable labels.

questions.title: Treat, wait, recheck
questions.question: An adult with diabetes is alert and reports shakiness and sweating. Their glucose reading is below the individual target. What should the nurse do first?
options: Repeat the glucose reading in an hour before giving anything
Give fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck the glucose after about fifteen minutes
Give a long-acting carbohydrate snack before the fast-acting one
Reduce the next dose of glucose-lowering medication without contacting the prescriber
questions.rationale: A conscious adult with hypoglycaemia is treated promptly with fast-acting carbohydrate, then the glucose is rechecked and followed by a longer-acting snack if the next meal is not imminent. Waiting an hour or substituting slow carbohydrate prolongs the hypo and risks deterioration.
questions.sourceTitle: NICE guideline NG17: Diabetes in adults - management
questions.learningObjective: Treat conscious hypoglycaemia with fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck promptly.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated bedside tray with a glucose meter and a glass of juice, labels blurred; no needles in skin and no readable numbers.

questions.title: Ten minutes to the trace
questions.question: An adult presents with sudden central chest pain. Which action should the nurse prioritise on arrival?
options: Ensuring a 12-lead electrocardiogram is obtained within about ten minutes of presentation
Offering food and fluids while awaiting a bed on the ward
Waiting until pain relief has worked before recording an electrocardiogram
Recording observations hourly unless the monitor shows a change
questions.rationale: Chest pain is assessed as a possible acute coronary syndrome until excluded, and a 12-lead ECG within ten minutes of presentation drives the immediate treatment pathway. Analgesia and comfort measures do not take precedence over the tracing.
questions.sourceTitle: NICE guideline CG95: Chest pain in acute coronary syndromes
questions.learningObjective: Prioritise a 12-lead ECG within ten minutes for acute chest pain.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated assessment bay with an ECG machine and leads laid out on an empty trolley, monitor screen deliberately blank; no patient.

questions.title: Two pairs of eyes for insulin
questions.question: Before administering insulin to an inpatient, which practice is expected for this high-alert medicine?
options: Checking the dose only when the patient asks a question about it
Relying on the pharmacy label alone, without checking the prescription
An independent double-check of the insulin type, strength, dose and device against the prescription
A quick glance at the pen label by whoever is handing over the dose
questions.rationale: Insulin is a high-alert medicine where a wrong type or strength causes serious harm, so an independent double-check of the product, dose and device against the prescription is expected before administration. A single unverified glance defeats the purpose of a double-check.
questions.sourceTitle: NICE guideline NG17: Diabetes in adults - management
questions.learningObjective: Apply an independent double-check before administering insulin.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated medication round with two nurses comparing an insulin pen and a prescription chart, all labels blurred and unreadable; no drug names.

questions.title: Twelve medicines and rising
questions.question: An older adult takes twelve regular medicines and mentions feeling drowsy and unsteady. What is the most appropriate first response?
options: Record the report and action it at the next annual review
Raise the possibility of a structured medication review with the prescriber or pharmacist
Advise the patient to stop the medicines that seem least important
Suggest taking an extra dose of the drowsiness-causing medicine at night
questions.rationale: New symptoms in a patient on many medicines warrant a structured medication review to identify adverse effects and deprescribing opportunities, led by the prescriber or pharmacist. Nurses must not advise stopping or changing doses independently, and waiting for an annual review leaves a falls risk unaddressed.
questions.sourceTitle: NICE guideline NG5: Medicines optimisation
questions.learningObjective: Escalate suspected medicine-related symptoms for a structured medication review.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated kitchen table covered with several unlabelled pill organisers and a blurred prescription envelope; no readable text.

questions.title: Sleepy is not pain-free
questions.question: A patient prescribed regular opioid analgesia is becoming increasingly drowsy between doses. What should the nurse do before the next dose is due?
options: Assess sedation and respiratory rate and withhold the dose, contacting the prescriber if the patient is excessively sedated
Give the next dose on schedule because the prescription says regular
Wake the patient fully and give the dose with a stimulant drink
Ask a relative to keep the patient awake so the dose can be given
questions.rationale: Increasing sedation precedes respiratory depression, so the nurse reassesses sedation and respiratory rate before each further opioid dose and withholds the dose for the prescriber's review when the patient is too sedated. A regular prescription never overrides an unsafe assessment.
questions.sourceTitle: Nursing Skills 2e (Open RN, WisTech Open, CC BY 4.0, 2023)
questions.learningObjective: Reassess sedation and respiration before every further opioid dose.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated observation chart folder beside a closed medication drawer, all markings blurred; a monitor with a deliberately blank screen; no people.

questions.title: Name the reaction
questions.question: A patient states they had a rash and swelling after penicillin as a child. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the prescribed penicillin anyway because the reaction was in childhood
Tell the patient the reaction probably does not matter if they feel well now
Record an allergy to all medicines as a precaution
Record the allergy and the specific reaction, and avoid penicillins and related medicines pending prescriber advice
questions.rationale: The allergy status and the nature of previous reactions must be documented clearly, and penicillins avoided unless a prescriber has explicitly assessed and cleared their use. Recording every medicine as an allergy, or dismissing the history, both create real clinical risk.
questions.sourceTitle: NICE guideline CG183: Drug allergy - diagnosis and management
questions.learningObjective: Document the allergy and its reaction, and avoid the allergic medicine class pending advice.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated wristband and folded chart on an empty bedside table with all lettering blurred; a red alert-style folder label without readable words.

questions.title: Ask plainly, then act
questions.question: A patient says life is not worth living. What is the best nursing response?
options: Promise the patient you will not tell anyone what they have said
Ask the patient directly and calmly whether they are having thoughts of suicide, then follow the local risk pathway
Avoid mentioning suicide directly in case it plants the idea
Change the subject to lighten the mood and note the comment in the record only
questions.rationale: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and is the recognised way to open an assessment; the answer then drives the local risk pathway and safety planning. Promising absolute secrecy is unsafe, and avoidance leaves the risk unassessed.
questions.sourceTitle: NICE guideline NG225: Self-harm - assessment, management and preventing recurrence
questions.learningObjective: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts and follow the risk pathway rather than avoiding the topic.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated quiet interview room with two empty chairs and a soft lamp, drawn warmly; no people and no readable material on the walls.

questions.title: Rule out the body first
questions.question: A patient reports sudden palpitations, chest tightness and a fear of dying. What should the nurse do first?
options: Stay with the patient, speak calmly, and complete a physical assessment to exclude physical causes
Assume a panic attack from the description and begin breathing exercises without assessment
Send the patient to wait in the corridor until they feel calmer
Explain that the symptoms cannot be real because tests are usually normal
questions.rationale: Physical causes such as arrhythmia, hypoxia and hypoglycaemia can mimic a panic attack, so a calm presence with a physical assessment comes first. Dismissing symptoms or leaving an acutely distressed patient alone is unsafe and damages trust.
questions.sourceTitle: NICE guideline CG113: Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults
questions.learningObjective: Assess and exclude physical causes before attributing acute distress to panic.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated assessment room with an observation monitor on a stand and a chair beside the bed, screen blank; no people.

questions.title: Consent can be refused
questions.question: A capacitous adult refuses a recommended blood transfusion even after the risks are explained. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask a relative to sign consent on the patient's behalf so treatment can proceed
Wait for the patient to be asleep and administer the transfusion then
Tell the patient the refusal will be ignored because it is life-saving
Respect the refusal, document the discussion and inform the team, because a capacitous adult may refuse treatment
questions.rationale: A capacitous adult has the right to refuse treatment for any reason, even when refusal may lead to serious harm, and that decision must be respected and documented. Relatives cannot consent for a capacitous adult, and treating without consent is unlawful.
questions.sourceTitle: Mental Capacity Act 2005 Code of Practice (UK Government)
questions.learningObjective: Respect and document a capacitous adult's informed refusal of treatment.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated quiet bedside conversation corner with a documentation folder and a cup of tea on a tray, text blurred; no people.

questions.title: Weigh the loss, call for help
questions.question: After a vaginal birth, bleeding appears heavier than expected. What should the midwife or nurse do first?
options: Change the pad each hour to see whether the trend continues
Wait for the next scheduled postnatal observations before acting
Quantify the blood loss, assess vital signs and tone, and escalate using the postpartum haemorrhage pathway
Estimate the loss by eye and document that it looks like more than usual
questions.rationale: Postpartum haemorrhage is managed by quantifying loss, assessing the mother's condition and triggering the local escalation pathway promptly, because underestimation by eye is a well-known cause of delayed treatment. Waiting or estimating loosely can let a manageable bleed become an emergency.
questions.sourceTitle: NICE guideline NG235: Intrapartum care
questions.learningObjective: Quantify postpartum blood loss and escalate immediately along the PPH pathway.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated delivery-room trolley with a graduated measuring jug, folded linen and a call bell, all clean and unlabelled; no people.

questions.title: Keep the first hours warm
questions.question: Which set of measures best prevents heat loss in a healthy newborn immediately after birth?
options: Bath the baby soon after birth so the skin is clean before contact
Keep the baby in a cot beside the bed with blankets until the mother feels ready
Leave the baby undressed under the radiant warmer for the whole first hour
Dry the baby promptly, encourage skin-to-skin contact with the mother, and delay the first bath
questions.rationale: Prompt drying, skin-to-skin contact and delaying the first bath conserve heat in the critical first hours, which protects the newborn's transition. Early bathing and unwrapped exposure increase heat loss, and separation from the mother for warmth is usually unnecessary.
questions.sourceTitle: NICE guideline NG204: Postnatal care
questions.learningObjective: Use drying, skin-to-skin contact and delayed bathing to keep a newborn warm.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated postnatal room with a warm blanket stack and a skin-to-skin chair beside a bassinet, drawn as a soft illustration; no identifiable faces.

questions.title: Watch a whole feed
questions.question: A first-time mother says breastfeeding is painful and the baby feeds often but seems unsettled. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Suggest limiting feeds to a strict four-hourly schedule
Observe a full feed to assess positioning and attachment, and offer skilled breastfeeding support
Advise topping up with formula until the baby seems satisfied
Tell her the pain settles on its own and no assessment is needed
questions.rationale: Pain and frequent unsettled feeding usually signal a positioning or attachment problem, so observing a whole feed and offering skilled support is the correct response. Unrequested formula top-ups and rigid schedules undermine establishing lactation and treat the symptom, not the cause.
questions.sourceTitle: NICE guideline NG204: Postnatal care
questions.learningObjective: Assess a full feed and offer skilled support rather than defaulting to top-ups.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated feeding-support room with a comfortable chair, support cushion and water glass on a side table; no people and no product labels.

questions.title: Weight first, dose second
questions.question: A prescription for a child is written in milligrams per kilogram. What must the nurse confirm before administering?
options: A dose estimated from the child's age band in the drug handbook
That an adult tablet formulation can be crushed to taste better
The child's current weight in kilograms and that the calculated dose is within the recommended milligram-per-kilogram range
The dose the child received at the previous admission, even if it was a year ago
questions.rationale: Paediatric doses are calculated from a current, measured weight in kilograms and checked against the recommended milligram-per-kilogram limits, because children's pharmacokinetics make fixed age-based estimates unsafe. Altering formulations without guidance can also change how the medicine works.
questions.sourceTitle: BNF for Children (NICE)
questions.learningObjective: Calculate and check paediatric doses against current weight and the milligram-per-kilogram limit.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated paediatric clinic room with a standing scale and a growth chart folder, all markings blurred; bright, friendly colours and no people.

questions.title: Talk with, not at
questions.question: A fourteen-year-old is admitted for day surgery and their parent answers every question on their behalf. What is the best approach?
options: Address the young person directly, use age-appropriate language and involve them in decisions in line with their understanding
Continue directing all information to the parent because the young person is a minor
Speak to the young person using simplified baby talk so they understand
Ask the parent to leave the room entirely for the whole admission
questions.rationale: Children and young people should be communicated with directly, in language that suits their age and understanding, and involved in decisions as far as they are able, with the parent still included. Excluding either the young person or the family entirely is poor practice.
questions.sourceTitle: NICE guideline NG245: Babies, children and young people's experience of healthcare
questions.learningObjective: Involve children and young people directly in communication and decisions about their care.
questions.visualBrief: Simulated hospital schoolroom corner with a games console, posters with unreadable graphics and a day-bed; friendly and uncluttered, no people.
